hook_text: When you light a gas stove, the gas seems to vanish. Not one atom of it is lost. Where does it all go?
clip_script: Turn on a gas stove and light it. The methane gas seems to vanish into a blue flame. But count the atoms. Each methane molecule is one carbon and four hydrogens. It meets two oxygen molecules from the air, four oxygen atoms. In the flame the bonds snap and the atoms swap partners. The carbon takes two oxygens and floats away as carbon dioxide. The hydrogens take the other two oxygens and float away as two molecules of water vapour. One carbon, four hydrogens, four oxygens before. One carbon, four hydrogens, four oxygens after. Nothing destroyed, nothing created, only rearranged. Breaking the old bonds needed a spark to start, but forming the new bonds released more energy, and that is the heat you cook with. Seal a reaction in a bottle and weigh it: the mass never changes.
visual_style: A whiteboard stove flame with zoomed-in coloured atom balls pulling apart and snapping into new molecules, a tally of atoms on each side, then a sealed bottle on a scale.
pacing: Steady counting with a satisfying final tally.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and count the atoms yourself.
